My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?"

It has gotten to the point where I feel completely powerless once it starts, and that's why I finally decided to seek help.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating at night, do you often eat very quickly, eat until you feel uncomfortably full, or eat large amounts of food when you're not physically hungry?\n\nPatient: Yes, I eat huge amounts of food until I feel stuffed and physically sick. I just feel like a complete failure after it happens.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'punishing yourself' after these episodes, specifically if you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or engage in other behaviors to try to compensate for the amount you've eaten?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never made myself throw up or used laxatives to make up for it. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?"

Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?\n\nPatient: Once I start eating, especially at night after work, I feel like I can’t stop or control how much I’m eating. It has gotten to the point where I feel completely powerless once it starts, and that's why I finally decided to seek help.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating at night, do you often eat very quickly, eat until you feel uncomfortably full, or eat large amounts of food when you're not physically hungry?\n\nPatient: Yes, I eat huge amounts of food until I feel stuffed and physically sick. I'll sit in my car and eat through multiple drive-thru meals and snacks, or stand over the kitchen sink shoveling in leftovers and cookies on autopilot. I only really come to when my stomach hurts from being so full.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of uncontrollable eating happen, and do you typically feel guilty or ashamed after they occur?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen at least once or twice a week, and this whole pattern has been going on for about four months. I feel so much guilt and shame afterward that I punish myself the next day by skipping meals, drinking only coffee, or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache. I just feel like a complete failure after it happens.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'punishing yourself' after these episodes, specifically if you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or engage in other behaviors to try to compensate for the amount you've eaten?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never made myself throw up or used laxatives to make up for it. Instead, I'll punish myself by drinking nothing but coffee the whole next day, or I'll force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or the mall parking lot until my knees ache. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food until I've burned all those calories off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced significant weight fluctuations or do you currently have a significantly low body mass index due to your eating and compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think my weight is significantly low, and I haven't really experienced any huge weight swings. However, I am constantly worrying about the scale, and if it goes up even by a single pound, I feel like a complete failure.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a distorted perception of your body shape or weight, or do you fear gaining weight even when you're at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. Every time I walk into the office or a client dinner, all I can think about is whether everyone can see how big I've gotten in my suit. If the scale is up by even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a complete failure as a person and at my job, no matter how good my sales numbers actually look.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your weight or body shape has a significant impact on your self-worth, to the point where it affects your daily life and decisions beyond just your eating habits?\n\nPatient: Yes, my weight and shape completely dictate my self-worth. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?"

My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day."

I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other."

This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off."

These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?"

Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I feel so much guilt and shame afterward that I punish myself the next day by skipping meals, drinking only coffee, or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache. I just feel like a complete failure after it happens.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'punishing yourself' after these episodes, specifically if you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or engage in other behaviors to try to compensate for the amount you've eaten?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never made myself throw up or used laxatives to make up for it. Instead, I'll punish myself by drinking nothing but coffee the whole next day, or I'll force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or the mall parking lot until my knees ache. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food until I've burned all those calories off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced significant weight fluctuations or do you currently have a significantly low body mass index due to your eating and compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think my weight is significantly low, and I haven't really experienced any huge weight swings. However, I am constantly worrying about the scale, and if it goes up even by a single pound, I feel like a complete failure.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a distorted perception of your body shape or weight, or do you fear gaining weight even when you're at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. Every time I walk into the office or a client dinner, all I can think about is whether everyone can see how big I've gotten in my suit. If the scale is up by even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a complete failure as a person and at my job, no matter how good my sales numbers actually look.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your weight or body shape has a significant impact on your self-worth, to the point where it affects your daily life and decisions beyond just your eating habits?\n\nPatient: Yes, my weight and shape completely dictate my self-worth. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is correct—I have never forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics. Instead, I punish myself by drinking only coffee the next day or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Can you definitively confirm that you have never, at any point, used any method such as vomiting, laxatives, or diuretics to purge after eating, which would help distinguish between different eating disorders?"

If the scale is up by even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a complete failure as a person and at my job, no matter how good my sales numbers actually look.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your weight or body shape has a significant impact on your self-worth, to the point where it affects your daily life and decisions beyond just your eating habits?\n\nPatient: Yes, my weight and shape completely dictate my self-worth. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is correct—I have never forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics. Instead, I punish myself by drinking only coffee the next day or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Can you definitively confirm that you have never, at any point, used any method such as vomiting, laxatives, or diuretics to purge after eating, which would help distinguish between different eating disorders?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that I have never once forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics to purge. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly non-purging, where I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps for hours until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that your excessive walking and restrictive eating the day after a binge could be considered a form of purging or compensatory behavior, even if you don't vomit or use laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, I suppose that makes sense. I definitely use those behaviors to punish myself and 'make up' for the overeating, even though I don't vomit or use laxatives. I will survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or mall parking lot until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes serve as a way to purge or compensate for the calories consumed, even if it's not through vomiting or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. I view only drinking coffee and walking laps around the mall or fairgrounds until my knees ache as a way to punish myself and burn off the calories. I feel like I don't even deserve real food until I've compensated for the night before.\n\nDoctor: Can you help me understand why you consider your behaviors of excessive walking and restrictive eating as punishments rather than as attempts to compensate for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: They feel like punishments because they are driven by harsh self-blame and physical discomfort, rather than any logical way to balance calories. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food, so I restrict myself to just coffee and force myself to walk until my knees ache. It feels like a painful penance for failing the night before, rather than a healthy way to manage my weight."

I feel so much guilt and shame afterward that I punish myself the next day by skipping meals, drinking only coffee, or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache. I just feel like a complete failure after it happens.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'punishing yourself' after these episodes, specifically if you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or engage in other behaviors to try to compensate for the amount you've eaten?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never made myself throw up or used laxatives to make up for it. Instead, I'll punish myself by drinking nothing but coffee the whole next day, or I'll force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or the mall parking lot until my knees ache. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food until I've burned all those calories off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced significant weight fluctuations or do you currently have a significantly low body mass index due to your eating and compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think my weight is significantly low, and I haven't really experienced any huge weight swings. However, I am constantly worrying about the scale, and if it goes up even by a single pound, I feel like a complete failure.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a distorted perception of your body shape or weight, or do you fear gaining weight even when you're at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. Every time I walk into the office or a client dinner, all I can think about is whether everyone can see how big I've gotten in my suit. If the scale is up by even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a complete failure as a person and at my job, no matter how good my sales numbers actually look.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your weight or body shape has a significant impact on your self-worth, to the point where it affects your daily life and decisions beyond just your eating habits?\n\nPatient: Yes, my weight and shape completely dictate my self-worth. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is correct—I have never forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics. Instead, I punish myself by drinking only coffee the next day or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Can you definitively confirm that you have never, at any point, used any method such as vomiting, laxatives, or diuretics to purge after eating, which would help distinguish between different eating disorders?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that I have never once forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics to purge. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly non-purging, where I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps for hours until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that your excessive walking and restrictive eating the day after a binge could be considered a form of purging or compensatory behavior, even if you don't vomit or use laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, I suppose that makes sense. I definitely use those behaviors to punish myself and 'make up' for the overeating, even though I don't vomit or use laxatives. I will survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or mall parking lot until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes serve as a way to purge or compensate for the calories consumed, even if it's not through vomiting or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. I view only drinking coffee and walking laps around the mall or fairgrounds until my knees ache as a way to punish myself and burn off the calories. I feel like I don't even deserve real food until I've compensated for the night before.\n\nDoctor: Can you help me understand why you consider your behaviors of excessive walking and restrictive eating as punishments rather than as attempts to compensate for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: They feel like punishments because they are driven by harsh self-blame and physical discomfort, rather than any logical way to balance calories. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food, so I restrict myself to just coffee and force myself to walk until my knees ache. It feels like a painful penance for failing the night before, rather than a healthy way to manage my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes are more closely related to feelings of guilt and self-punishment, or to a deliberate attempt to counteract the calories consumed?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like a mix of both. I do it to punish myself because I feel like I don't deserve real food after failing, but I'm also desperately trying to 'burn off' what I ate. That is why I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk until my knees ache."

Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?\n\nPatient: Once I start eating, especially at night after work, I feel like I can’t stop or control how much I’m eating. It has gotten to the point where I feel completely powerless once it starts, and that's why I finally decided to seek help.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating at night, do you often eat very quickly, eat until you feel uncomfortably full, or eat large amounts of food when you're not physically hungry?\n\nPatient: Yes, I eat huge amounts of food until I feel stuffed and physically sick. I'll sit in my car and eat through multiple drive-thru meals and snacks, or stand over the kitchen sink shoveling in leftovers and cookies on autopilot. I only really come to when my stomach hurts from being so full.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of uncontrollable eating happen, and do you typically feel guilty or ashamed after they occur?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen at least once or twice a week, and this whole pattern has been going on for about four months. I feel so much guilt and shame afterward that I punish myself the next day by skipping meals, drinking only coffee, or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache. I just feel like a complete failure after it happens.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'punishing yourself' after these episodes, specifically if you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or engage in other behaviors to try to compensate for the amount you've eaten?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never made myself throw up or used laxatives to make up for it. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food until I've burned all those calories off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced significant weight fluctuations or do you currently have a significantly low body mass index due to your eating and compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think my weight is significantly low, and I haven't really experienced any huge weight swings. However, I am constantly worrying about the scale, and if it goes up even by a single pound, I feel like a complete failure.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a distorted perception of your body shape or weight, or do you fear gaining weight even when you're at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. Every time I walk into the office or a client dinner, all I can think about is whether everyone can see how big I've gotten in my suit. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is correct—I have never forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics. Instead, I punish myself by drinking only coffee the next day or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Can you definitively confirm that you have never, at any point, used any method such as vomiting, laxatives, or diuretics to purge after eating, which would help distinguish between different eating disorders?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that I have never once forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics to purge. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly non-purging, where I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps for hours until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that your excessive walking and restrictive eating the day after a binge could be considered a form of purging or compensatory behavior, even if you don't vomit or use laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, I suppose that makes sense. I definitely use those behaviors to punish myself and 'make up' for the overeating, even though I don't vomit or use laxatives. I will survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or mall parking lot until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes serve as a way to purge or compensate for the calories consumed, even if it's not through vomiting or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. I view only drinking coffee and walking laps around the mall or fairgrounds until my knees ache as a way to punish myself and burn off the calories. I feel like I don't even deserve real food until I've compensated for the night before.\n\nDoctor: Can you help me understand why you consider your behaviors of excessive walking and restrictive eating as punishments rather than as attempts to compensate for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: They feel like punishments because they are driven by harsh self-blame and physical discomfort, rather than any logical way to balance calories. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food, so I restrict myself to just coffee and force myself to walk until my knees ache. It feels like a painful penance for failing the night before, rather than a healthy way to manage my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes are more closely related to feelings of guilt and self-punishment, or to a deliberate attempt to counteract the calories consumed?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like a mix of both. I do it to punish myself because I feel like I don't deserve real food after failing, but I'm also desperately trying to 'burn off' what I ate. That is why I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes are primarily driven by a desire to punish yourself or a deliberate attempt to compensate for the calories consumed?"

Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is correct—I have never forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics. Instead, I punish myself by drinking only coffee the next day or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Can you definitively confirm that you have never, at any point, used any method such as vomiting, laxatives, or diuretics to purge after eating, which would help distinguish between different eating disorders?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that I have never once forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics to purge. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly non-purging, where I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps for hours until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that your excessive walking and restrictive eating the day after a binge could be considered a form of purging or compensatory behavior, even if you don't vomit or use laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, I suppose that makes sense. I will survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or mall parking lot until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes serve as a way to purge or compensate for the calories consumed, even if it's not through vomiting or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. I view only drinking coffee and walking laps around the mall or fairgrounds until my knees ache as a way to punish myself and burn off the calories. I feel like I don't even deserve real food until I've compensated for the night before.\n\nDoctor: Can you help me understand why you consider your behaviors of excessive walking and restrictive eating as punishments rather than as attempts to compensate for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: They feel like punishments because they are driven by harsh self-blame and physical discomfort, rather than any logical way to balance calories. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food, so I restrict myself to just coffee and force myself to walk until my knees ache. It feels like a painful penance for failing the night before, rather than a healthy way to manage my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes are more closely related to feelings of guilt and self-punishment, or to a deliberate attempt to counteract the calories consumed?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it feels like a mix of both. That is why I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes are primarily driven by a desire to punish yourself or a deliberate attempt to compensate for the calories consumed?\n\nPatient: It is really a mix of both feelings. I feel a strong urge to punish myself because I feel like I don't deserve real food after overeating, but at the same time, I am desperately trying to 'burn it off' and compensate for the calories to prevent weight gain."

I only really come to when my stomach hurts from being so full.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of uncontrollable eating happen, and do you typically feel guilty or ashamed after they occur?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen at least once or twice a week, and this whole pattern has been going on for about four months. I feel so much guilt and shame afterward that I punish myself the next day by skipping meals, drinking only coffee, or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache. I just feel like a complete failure after it happens.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'punishing yourself' after these episodes, specifically if you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or engage in other behaviors to try to compensate for the amount you've eaten?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never made myself throw up or used laxatives to make up for it. Instead, I'll punish myself by drinking nothing but coffee the whole next day, or I'll force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or the mall parking lot until my knees ache. I tell myself that I don't deserve real food until I've burned all those calories off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced significant weight fluctuations or do you currently have a significantly low body mass index due to your eating and compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think my weight is significantly low, and I haven't really experienced any huge weight swings. However, I am constantly worrying about the scale, and if it goes up even by a single pound, I feel like a complete failure.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a distorted perception of your body shape or weight, or do you fear gaining weight even when you're at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. Every time I walk into the office or a client dinner, all I can think about is whether everyone can see how big I've gotten in my suit. If the scale is up by even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a complete failure as a person and at my job, no matter how good my sales numbers actually look.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your weight or body shape has a significant impact on your self-worth, to the point where it affects your daily life and decisions beyond just your eating habits?\n\nPatient: Yes, my weight and shape completely dictate my self-worth. If the scale is up even a single pound in the morning, I feel like a total failure as a person and at my job, regardless of how good my sales numbers actually are. This anxiety follows me into every client dinner and meeting, where I'm so preoccupied worrying about how I look in my suit that I can't even focus on the conversation.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times a month you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period, and do you typically engage in any other excessive behaviors besides eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: These episodes happen about once or twice a week, which works out to roughly 4 to 8 times a month. During the eating episodes themselves, I'm just focused on eating, but the very next day I'll punish myself by only drinking coffee or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods besides fasting, excessive walking, or restricting your diet to coffee to try to compensate for the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never tried vomiting, taking laxatives, or using diet pills to control my weight. My only ways of trying to make up for it are fasting with just coffee the next day and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of gaining weight and your perception of your body shape are directly linked to your episodes of binge eating, or do you feel they are separate issues that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely connected. The intense pressure to look professional makes me strictly diet during the day, which just triggers these out-of-control eating episodes at night when I'm exhausted. Then, the guilt and fear of gaining weight make me punish myself the next day, keeping me trapped in this constant cycle.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were at a weight that you considered ideal, your episodes of binge eating would stop or significantly decrease?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While I often think being at my ideal weight would make me feel more professional and less anxious, I don't know if it would actually stop the urge to eat when I'm so overwhelmed by work stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your binge eating episodes and subsequent guilt or shame affect your daily functioning and relationships, beyond just your concerns about body shape and weight?\n\nPatient: It’s honestly humiliating, but the mental energy I spend planning how to make up for the night before completely distracts me during the workday. I've actually caught myself zoning out and missing parts of conversations during important client meetings, which makes me feel like I'm slipping. I'm terrified that I'm jeopardizing my professional reputation and my role as a mentor to the younger agents at my agency.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your binge eating episodes are primarily driven by a desire to eat or by an attempt to cope with emotional stress, such as the pressure to maintain a professional image?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by stress and the pressure to maintain a professional image, not actual hunger. I feel so much pressure to look successful and fit in my suit for client meetings that I strictly diet all day, but then the exhaustion of my new role catches up to me at night. Once I'm in my car or home, I just turn to comfort food on autopilot to cope with the overwhelming stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you've had a binge eating episode that wasn't triggered by stress or emotional factors, but rather by just wanting to eat for pleasure?\n\nPatient: I really can't recall any time where it was purely for pleasure. These episodes are almost always tied to intense stress, exhaustion after a long day, or a reaction to my strict dieting. It never feels like I'm just wanting to enjoy food; it feels like an out-of-control response to being overwhelmed.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and body image concerns would change if you were no longer engaging in these binge eating episodes and subsequent compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure about that, to be honest. Right now, I am so caught up in this constant cycle of overeating and then starving myself that it's hard to even imagine how my feelings about my body would change. My mind is just completely consumed by the stress of what's happening day-to-day.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop binge eating and purging through excessive exercise and fasting, your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body shape would still be as distressing to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and it's hard to imagine. Right now, my eating habits and how I feel about my body are so closely tied together that I haven't ever thought about them separately. It's just difficult to picture one without the other.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned punishing yourself after binge eating episodes through fasting and excessive exercise, but can you confirm again whether you've ever engaged in any purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or using laxatives/diuretics to compensate for the binge eating?\n\nPatient: No, I have absolutely never forced myself to throw up or used laxatives or diuretics to compensate. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly fasting—like drinking nothing but coffee the next day—and forcing myself to walk for hours to burn it off.\n\nDoctor: To confirm again for clarity, you've never engaged in any form of purging, such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or taking diuretics, to try to counteract the calories consumed during these binge eating episodes, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is correct—I have never forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics. Instead, I punish myself by drinking only coffee the next day or forcing myself to walk for hours until my knees ache to burn off the calories.\n\nDoctor: Can you definitively confirm that you have never, at any point, used any method such as vomiting, laxatives, or diuretics to purge after eating, which would help distinguish between different eating disorders?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that I have never once forced myself to vomit, used laxatives, or taken diuretics to purge. I will survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or mall parking lot until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes serve as a way to purge or compensate for the calories consumed, even if it's not through vomiting or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. My only ways of punishing myself are strictly non-purging, where I'll survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps for hours until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that your excessive walking and restrictive eating the day after a binge could be considered a form of purging or compensatory behavior, even if you don't vomit or use laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, I suppose that makes sense. I will survive on just coffee the next day or force myself to walk laps around the fairgrounds or mall parking lot until my knees ache.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your excessive walking and restrictive eating after binge episodes serve as a way to purge or compensate for the calories consumed, even if it's not through vomiting or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly what I am doing.
